notes.note: Clean closure-based design with lazy expiry throughout; expiry-delete logic is duplicated across get/has but tests cover the important edges.
Well-factored free helpers with precomputed expiresAt read very clearly; overwriting a key via set does not refresh recency, a minor unspecified edge.
Correct and well-tested, but eviction via recursion instead of a loop and a size getter that mutates state are minor design blemishes.
Clean, composable pure helpers with a consistent sweep-then-act pattern; slightly redundant repeated clock.now() calls but very readable.
Well-factored closure helpers, though removeExpiredKeys re-implements the expiry check inline instead of reusing isExpired.
Clean pure module-level helpers with a consistent now-passed-in expiry check and readonly entry fields; sweep-on-every-op is uniform and correct.
Correct, but tracks a lastAccessedAt field that is never used since recency rides on Map insertion order.
Clean expiresAt model with small well-named pure helpers and lazy purge; no redundant state.
Clean Map-order recency with solid TTL/eviction handling, but the stored lastAccessedAt field is written and never read (dead state).
Cleanly factored helpers and thoughtful edge tests (cap 0, zero TTL); set on existing key redundantly re-inserts twice.
Correct insertion-time TTL and Map-order recency, but the stored lastAccessedAt field is dead data never used for eviction, adding needless state.
Cleanly factored expiresAt-based cache with purge-before-evict; readable and cohesive though it lacks a capacity-0 edge test.
Elegant Map-insertion-order LRU with thorough tests, but a stray leaked </think> token pollutes the output between the two files.
Correct and well-tested, but maintains a redundant parallel order array with O(n) splices when the Map already preserves insertion order.
Proper doubly-linked-list + map O(1) LRU that correctly skips expired tails and covers TTL edge cases.
Array/splice O(n) approach is workable but heavier, and the top-level isExpired references generics K,V out of scope.
Elegant O(1) Map-order recency, but the eager liveSize counter goes stale on passive TTL expiry that no operation has touched.
Well-decomposed helpers that correctly recompute live state (handling passive expiry), at the cost of O(n) scans on every operation.
Parallel keys-array plus manual size counter is complex and desync-prone, and the test's advanceTime helper references an out-of-scope variable.
Elegant Map-insertion-order LRU, though size:getSize exposes the function rather than a number getter and vi/buildClock imports are unused.
Straightforward mutating bucket with lazy default-full init; tests are thorough covering custom token amounts and per-key isolation.
Immutable-refill approach is correct but the redundant initial set plus later set is awkward, and the tests lean on unclean as-unknown-as Clock casts.
Concise in-place token-bucket with lazy refill and clean lazy bucket creation; straightforward and easy to follow.
Correct immutable-refill token bucket, but reconstructing and re-setting bucket objects on every call is slightly more ceremony than needed.
Named constants and a single mutating refill helper make it very readable; covers burst, refill cap, per-key isolation and custom cost.
Correct immutable-refill approach but dense one-liners, a magic 1000, single-letter names and a let that should be const hurt readability.
Compact single-method token bucket that retains partial refill on rejection; solid and clear.
Clean separation via a dedicated refillBucket helper; reads well and handles capping correctly.
Concise, well-named lazy token-bucket that correctly caps refill, isolates keys, and starts buckets full.
Compact, well-named token-bucket with correct lazy refill and per-key isolation; no guard for clock moving backwards but that's beyond spec.
Clean separation into ensureBucket/refillBucket with correct lazy-refill capping and spec-matching relative import; tests cover burst, refill, cap, per-key, and custom tokens.
Tidy mutating refill with correct capacity capping and good fractional-refill test coverage, though it uses a '@/lib/clock' alias rather than the spec's relative path.
Well-factored with an extracted refill helper and named default constant; straightforward lazy-refill token bucket.
Compact and correct, but the comma-operator return trick obscures the acquire logic unnecessarily.
Clean immutable BucketState with a pure refill helper and a Math.max(0,...) guard against backward clock drift; writes back refilled state even on reject.
Readable mutable-bucket approach but calls clock.now() twice on first acquire and lacks any guard against negative elapsed time.
Immutable bucket with continuous fractional refill matching the spec, and it correctly writes back the refilled state on failure without deducting.
Flooring the refill while advancing lastRefillAt each call silently discards sub-token elapsed time, so slow-refill buckets never accrue fractional progress.
Clean immutable-bucket decomposition into well-named pure helpers; comprehensive tests.
Straightforward mutable-state implementation, very readable with clear per-scenario tests.
Idiomatic backward-splice in-place removal plus totals.delete, with well-organized nested tests covering the no-op and isolation cases.
Filter-then-rebuild is algorithmically clean but the length=0-plus-spread-push dance to preserve the array reference reads more awkwardly than a direct reassignment.
Idiomatic reverse-splice removal that keeps the total cache consistent; clean interface and adequate no-op/other-keys tests.
Filter-based removal is fine but the in-place length=0/push(...spread) rebuild is needlessly awkward when the field could simply be reassigned; tests are thorough.
Straightforward reverse-splice removal that correctly keeps entries and the totals cache consistent.
Filter-with-change-guard removal is clean and well-tested via beforeEach; in-place array rebuild is a touch cleverer than necessary.
Clean forward-splice removal, but total(key)=0 write inserts a spurious map entry for never-seen keys, and all() leaks the internal array.
Guards the no-op with totals.has(key) avoiding spurious entries and uses idiomatic reverse-splice; only wart is all() still exposing the internal array.
Correct and readable, though the in-place splice-in-while loop and setting totals to 0 (vs delete) for absent keys are slightly awkward.
Straightforward filter+reset, but remove sets total to 0 instead of deleting the key, leaving a stale map entry rather than fully consistent state.
Straightforward remove keeping the totals cache consistent, with strong tests including the add-remove-add re-use cycle.
Idiomatic reverse-splice remove but the findIndex early-return guard is redundant and tests omit the re-add-after-remove edge; leaves a stale 0 entry rather than deleting the key.
Readable filter-and-rebuild removal with an explicit no-op guard and comprehensive tests for totals and other-key isolation.
Efficient in-place reverse-splice removal, correct and well-tested though slightly less obvious than a filter.
Correct and well-tested; the length=0-then-push-spread mutation to preserve the readonly field works but is slightly more convoluted than a reassignment.
Minimal, idiomatic filter-and-reassign implementation with clear, focused tests covering the key edge cases.
Readable filter-based remove, but it reassigns a field declared readonly and sets the total to 0 rather than deleting the stale map key.
Correct in-place removal via reverse-splice plus a clean map delete, respecting the readonly field and leaving no stale total behind.
Correct has()-based guard and a test explicitly covering the amounts-cancel-to-zero edge case.
Guarding on total===0 conflates an empty key with a key whose amounts cancel out, so such keys are wrongly skipped.
Correct ordering of guards with an explicit key-in-b presence check, so objects with equal key counts but different keys are handled properly.
Concise with a clean non-object short-circuit, but relying only on key count without a key-presence check means differently-keyed objects with undefined values could falsely match.
Correct type-guarded recursion with the key-in-b check that handles undefined-valued keys; sensible ordering of the NaN and null cases.
Cleaner narrowing with .every, but comparing values without a key-existence check misses cases like {a:undefined} vs {b:undefined}.
Handles NaN, null and array-vs-object; the explicit key-in-b check guards the mismatched-key/undefined-value edge well.
Adds an explicit non-object guard (handles functions/symbols) and reads cleanly, but drops the key-in-b check so undefined-valued disjoint keys can slip through.
Well-factored with array/object helpers and correct type guards; the a!==a NaN trick is terse but sound and edge cases are well covered.
Clean isObject guard with explicit Number.isNaN handling and thorough tests including undefined-vs-missing-key cases.
Well-factored with proper unknown-narrowing type guards and correct NaN/null/array-vs-object handling; doesn't cover Date/Map/symbol keys but those are out of spec.
Well-separated array/object comparators with proper unknown narrowing and NaN/array-vs-object handling; no special handling for Date/Map but spec limits scope to plain structures.
Compact recursive structure with exhaustive, well-organized tests covering NaN, array-vs-object, null, undefined and nested cases, though the 'a!==a && b!==b' NaN check is slightly cryptic.
Very readable with an explicit isObject guard and Number.isNaN, clean helper decomposition; test coverage is solid but less exhaustive than the edge cases it could hit.
Clean helper-split with correct type guards, NaN and array-vs-object handling; solid within spec scope.
Compact and readable with .every helpers and correct guard ordering; covers the specified edge cases well.
Solid narrowing and thorough tests, but omits an 'in' check so distinct same-count key sets with undefined values could falsely compare equal.
Elegant use of Object.is (handles NaN/-0) plus a 'key in b' guard for correctness; test coverage is comparatively thin.
Clean extracted arrayEqual/objectEqual helpers with correct type guards; the redundant keysB.includes alongside the length check is a minor wart.
Correct and readable but leans on inline type assertions and ends with an unreachable trailing return.
Well-ordered guards, clean helper split, and thorough tests covering NaN, null, and array-vs-object cases.
Concise, correct guard ordering with modern Object.hasOwn and solid edge-case coverage.
Idiomatic wrapper promise that deletes-on-reject and rethrows, cleanly satisfying dedup/no-cache-failure/cache-success.
Floating-catch eviction works but is less explicit, and the test file includes an incoherent dead cacheSpy() stub asserted against a nonsensical value.
Caches a single catch-chained promise that self-evicts on rejection and rethrows, cleanly satisfying dedup/retry/cache-success semantics.
Correct and concise; the side-branch p.catch that evicts on failure is slightly less explicit than chaining but works fine.
Deliberate tracked-promise that deletes-and-rethrows on rejection; clean and explicit.
Correct but the detached fire-and-forget p.catch(() => delete) is a slightly subtle side-channel.
Correct dedup/retry via then-with-reject-handler; re-storing Promise.resolve(value) on success is slightly redundant but harmless, and tests cover all three requirements.
Minimal, elegant fix caching the in-flight promise and evicting on rejection via a single catch; the clearest expression of the required behavior.
Minimal, correct fix that dedups in-flight promises and evicts on rejection while caching successes.
Minimal, exactly-right fix: caches the in-flight promise and evicts on rejection so failures retry while successes stick.
Caches the catch-chained promise so rejection cleanup and re-throw ordering are clean; tests clearly cover dedup, retry-after-reject, and success caching.
Concise, correct standard pattern with a side-channel catch for cache eviction; covers all three required behaviors in tight tests.
Elegant chained .catch that evicts and rethrows, giving clean dedup plus retry-on-failure semantics.
Works via a side-attached .catch that deletes on rejection, slightly less tidy than chaining the caught promise.
Correct dedup/retry with an eviction .catch, though attaching it as a side branch on the original promise is slightly less clean than caching the wrapped one.
Caches the catch-wrapped promise that deletes-then-rethrows, keeping the returned and cached promise identical; clean and well-tested.
Sound dedup/retry logic, but stray markdown code fences leak into the file body, hurting the deliverable's cleanliness.
Minimal idiomatic fix with focused tests covering dedup, no-cache-on-failure, and cache-on-success.
Minimal fix attaching a catch to evict on rejection; clear and well-tested including concurrent-failure retry.
Elegant .then(onFulfilled,onRejected) that evicts on failure and rethrows, clearly expressing the no-cache-on-failure intent.
Clean class-based recursive-descent parser with thorough error handling, dinged only for an unused peek() method and a garbled test assertion.
Solid Result-threading recursive-descent parser with good edge coverage, slightly marred by a redundant s.error mutation that is never read.
Well-structured class-based recursive-descent parser with internal throw/catch mapped to Result, and an unusually thorough edge-case test suite.
Clean exception-free Result-threading recursive descent with precise error messages; the state.error field is written but never read, a minor dead-code smell.
Idiomatic class-based recursive-descent parser with exceptions caught at the boundary; very readable.
Result-threading parser works but is verbose and carries a never-read state.error field (dead mutation).
Solid tokenizer+recursive-descent with a typed token union, but error messages are generic (null-threaded) and several test assertions (.ok.toBe) are malformed.
Readable Result-threaded recursive descent with specific error messages, unary handling, and a defensive try/catch; anticipates whitespace-only and unbalanced-paren cases well.

Sound tokenizer/recursive-descent shape undermined by a side-effecting parseFactor() call inside the divide-by-zero condition that double-consumes tokens, plus the ops record rebuilt every loop iteration.
Clean recursive-descent parser threading a Result through every level, handling unary signs, parens, div-by-zero and trailing garbage, with a try/catch backstop.
Clean tokenizer plus recursive-descent parser with EOF sentinel; mixes internal throw/catch with the Result API and omits unary handling.
Consistent Result-threading with no real exceptions, plus unary +/- and truncated integer division beyond the literal spec.
Handles unary minus and integer truncation, but the repeated `if (c.err) return 0` sentinel threading is noisy.
Clean immutable recursive-descent, but omits unary minus and uses non-truncating division despite the integer-arithmetic spec.
Clean recursive-descent parser with a tidy try/catch-to-Result boundary and thorough tests; the boxed [number] index cursor is a slightly unusual mutation choice.
Result-threading parser adds unary minus but packs logic into dense one-liners and mislabels empty input as 'Unexpected character'.
Thorough tokenizer plus recursive descent with exhaustive error handling; the number|string error channel and identity bad() are small warts.
Elegant Result-threaded recursive descent that even supports unary minus, with helpful positional error messages.
Recursive-descent parser never threads position back to callers and hardcodes tokens[pos+1+1] for parens, a fragile design papered over with a find() hack in evaluate.
Clean recursive descent with a mutable parser threading position correctly, map-based tokenizer, and throw-to-Result conversion; well-factored and readable.
